summary: This Wikipedia article defines cross slope (also called cross fall or camber), the transverse slope of pavement surfaces relative to the horizon. It explains that cross slope provides drainage so water runs off to gutters or ditches, and that on curves it is banked as superelevation to reduce steering effort and lateral force. Typical values range from 2 percent on straight segments to 10 percent on sharp superelevated curves.
one_line: Cross slope, or camber, is the transverse pavement slope that drains water off roads and banks curves for safer driving.
key_facts: Cross slope, also called cross fall or camber, is the transverse slope of a pavement surface with respect to the horizon.
Cross slope is described as a very important safety factor.
Cross slope provides a drainage gradient so water runs off the surface to a drainage system such as a street gutter or ditch.
Inadequate cross slope will contribute to aquaplaning.
On straight sections of normal two-lane roads, the pavement cross section is usually highest in the center and drains to both sides.
In horizontal curves, the cross slope is banked into superelevation to reduce steering effort and lateral force required to go around the curve.
All water drains to the inside of the curve.
If the cross slope magnitude oscillates within 1–25 metres (3–82 ft), the body and payload of high (heavy) vehicles will experience high roll vibration.
Cross slope is usually expressed as a percentage: rise divided by run, times 100%.
Typical cross slope values range from 2 percent for straight segments to 10 percent for sharp superelevated curves.
Cross slope may also be expressed as a fraction of an inch in rise over a one-foot run, for example 1/4 inch per foot.
The article's cross section figure of a road labels a gutter, shoulder, sub-base, base course and asphalt.
Cited references include a Tennessee Department of Transportation Superelevation Design Guide dated 23 January 2023 and a WSDOT Cross Slope and Superelevation manual section.
The article is categorized under Pavement engineering and was last edited on 23 January 2023.
